chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Playing for the love of it
summary: Wilson says he and Hinton would have played for nothing, since jam sessions were payment enough, and jazz big bands have yet to flower fully.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: Yeah, but there's something about our music that made us do it, we would have played that stuff, Milt, even if we didn't get paid.

We did, true. We could get from one to two thousand dollars for one hour's work if you were in the right spot, like for TV or something like that, and yet you can play for two bucks, or play for nothing -- you can play for a benefit, but even if we could not have been paid, the jam sessions would have been pay enough.
I mean, you and I have sat in on thousands of jam sessions and would play until daylight for nothing.

And Steven, you play a lot for nothing, don't you, playing in sessions with young musicians? So there is something about it that's basically good. You see, that will keep it alive. In other words, we are not 100% dependent on the buck to do this.

We're gonna do it -- we got to do it, even if we have to make a buck some other way, we're going to play the jazz music. It is such a valid and good thing. And I do feel that those big jazz bands, and those fellows that have been lagging, except for Duke and Fletcher and a few others, with a pencil and paper, to put this stuff on paper, that still has got to flower and hit its heyday.
